An apostle is one of the twelve followers of Jesus chosen as his closest companions and primary witnesses to his ministry. The word comes from Greek and literally means "one sent forth." After the Resurrection, these apostles became the foundation of the early Christian Church and shaped its theology and practice. The twelve traditionally include Peter, James, John, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the Less, Judas, Simon, and Thaddeus, though different gospels vary slightly on the exact membership. Peter emerged as the chief apostle and became the leader of the Jerusalem church after Jesus's death. Paul, though not one of the original twelve, claimed apostolic authority as a direct witness to the risen Jesus. These apostles performed miracles, baptized converts, and spread Christianity throughout the Mediterranean world, though many were imprisoned and eventually martyred for their faith. The apostolic age ended with the death of the last apostle in the late first century, marking a transition to second-generation Christian leadership. The doctrine of apostolic succession, which holds that authority passes directly from the apostles through a continuous chain of bishops, became foundational to Catholic and Orthodox church governance.
